question: An engineer on your team will use the agent to build a function that normalizes phone numbers from a legacy CRM export into one standard format. The function must handle empty fields, international prefixes, and numbers with extensions. It must also process one million records within a nightly time limit. Earlier agent-written utilities passed review but failed on unusual input in production. Which approach gives the most reliable progressive improvement?

options.text: Before implementation, write tests for expected outputs, edge cases such as empty fields and extensions, and the nightly time limit, then share each round's test failures with the agent.
options.reason: The guide recommends writing a test suite first that covers expected behavior, edge cases, and performance requirements. You then iterate by sharing the test failures, which guides progressive improvement.

options.text: Ask the agent to state its confidence that each edge case is handled, and accept the version once it reports high confidence for every case.
options.reason: Self-reported confidence does not check behavior against expected outputs or performance requirements. The guide's method is to iterate on actual test failures.

options.text: Write a detailed prose specification that describes every phone format and edge case, have the agent implement it in one pass, and then spot-check a few hundred converted records by hand afterward.
options.reason: The guide notes that prose descriptions can be interpreted inconsistently. A single pass with manual spot checks gives no test failures to share, so there is no reliable progressive iteration.

options.text: Have the agent implement the normalizer first, then generate tests from that code so the suite records its current behavior as correct.
options.reason: The guide says to write tests before implementation. Tests generated from finished code only lock in existing defects and cannot guide improvement.
